summary: For ages 8–9, learners construct a simple series circuit and name its parts (cell/battery, wire, bulb, switch, buzzer), with the central organising idea being the COMPLETE LOOP: a bulb lights only when there is an unbroken path from one terminal of the cell, through the components, back to the other terminal. This is a hands-on procedure plus vocabulary, not current theory. Physical construction with a real kit is the primary aim; a snap-together on-screen builder is a strong companion for topology, vocabulary and procedure rehearsal but does not replace the physical build the curriculum requires.
misconceptions: Unipolar / 'one wire' model: a single wire from the battery to the bulb is enough to light it — children ignore the return path.
Clashing-currents model: electricity comes out of BOTH ends of the cell and meets/fights at the bulb to light it.
'The bulb just needs to touch the battery' — not understanding that the path must run through the bulb's two separate contacts.
Confusing 'cell' and 'battery' is fine, but thinking the holder or the wire is the source of power is not — the cell is the source.
Believing more wires or a bigger tangle means more power; circuit topology, not amount of wire, decides whether it lights.

activities.title: Build the loop with a real kit
steps: Using real components (cell in a holder, wires with crocodile clips, a bulb in a holder, a switch, a buzzer), build a circuit that lights the bulb or sounds the buzzer.
Name each part out loud as you place it: cell (battery), wire, bulb, switch, buzzer.
Trace the path with your finger starting at one terminal of the cell, through the components, and check it returns to the other terminal.

If it doesn't light, work through a fault-finding checklist: is the bulb screwed into its holder? Is the crocodile clip on bare metal, not plastic insulation? Is the cell flat? Is a wire loose or the switch open?
Once it works, remove one wire, predict what will happen, then check.
activities.insight: A bulb lights only when the current has a complete, unbroken loop back to the cell; both terminals of the cell and both separate contacts of the bulb must be joined into the loop. Many faults are breaks found by tracing the loop, but a flat cell or blown bulb can leave the bulb dark even when the wires form a loop.

activities.title: Snap-together circuit playground (digital companion)
steps: Drag a cell, two wires and a bulb onto a board and click them end to end; watch the bulb glow the instant the loop closes and go dark if any join is pulled apart.
Start by running just ONE wire from the cell to the bulb, notice it stays dark, then add the return wire to the cell's other terminal and see it light.
Read each part's name as it lands ('cell', 'bulb', 'switch', 'buzzer').
Use a 'show the path' toggle that traces the live loop with a moving dot so the unbroken circle is visible.

Explore variations and report what each actually does: a clip on plastic insulation and a flat cell leave the bulb dark, while a reversed single cell still lights it — reversing a cell does not break the loop (a filament bulb is non-polar). Polarity changes behaviour only for a buzzer (which may fall silent reversed) or a motor (which reverses its direction of turn), not for the bulb.
activities.insight: It is the complete loop — not the bulb merely touching the battery — that lights the bulb; closing or breaking the loop is directly felt through the live bulb state.

activities.title: Name and order the parts (vocabulary & procedure support)
steps: On a finished circuit, tap each part to reveal its name and what it does (cell, wire, bulb/lamp, switch, buzzer).
Match each conventional circuit symbol to the real part it stands for, introduced as a name-tag for a part already handled.
Put the steps of building a circuit into the correct order.
Choose which of several loops would light (e.g. identify the closed loop versus a broken one).
activities.insight: Secure the names and jobs of components and the sequence of building, linking symbols to the physical things they label.

checkQuestion: Here's a cell, two wires, a bulb and a switch. Build a circuit that lights the bulb. As you go, tell me what each part is — and if it doesn't light, find and fix the problem. [Watch: do they form a complete loop from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, back to the other terminal, connecting BOTH bulb contacts?]
checkAnswer: Connects the components in a complete loop — both terminals of the cell joined through the wires, switch and bulb, with the bulb wired into the loop at its two separate contacts — so the bulb lights; names cell, wire, bulb and switch; and when it fails, traces the loop to find the break (loose wire, single connection to the bulb, open switch).
